prompt: What did Renata keep when she sent Paula the first, task-shaped message?
hint: The lesson’s phrase: she kept one thing and handed over another.

choices.text: The deadline, which she left out of the message on purpose
choices.why: The deadline is not what the lesson says she kept; the task message did lack one, but that is not the point made.

choices.text: The contact with the clinics who complained about the duplicates
choices.why: Helena held the complaints, and the outcome message pointed Paula to her.

choices.text: The thinking
choices.why: Right: the diagnosis, the design and the estimate were all hers, and Paula got the typing.

choices.text: The code review of whatever Paula wrote
choices.why: Review is not mentioned as what she kept; she kept the decisions about cause and design.

prompt: Which of these is an outcome rather than a task?

choices.text: Add an index on the appointments table
choices.why: It names a table and a technique, so the design has been decided.

choices.text: Move the history query to the read replica so the primary is less loaded at peak times
choices.why: A mechanism with a reason attached is still a mechanism.

choices.text: Cache the patient history in Redis
choices.why: It names a tool and a design.

choices.text: Clinics see a patient’s full history within two seconds
choices.why: Right: it says what has to be true and leaves the how open.

prompt: Why would the task version of the reminders fix have left the problem half solved?
hint: Where did the duplicates actually come from?

choices.text: Most duplicates came from reschedules made more than a day ahead, which the 24-hour check would miss
choices.why: Right: the cause was rescheduling, and a check on `sent_at` within a day misses every reschedule made further ahead.

choices.text: Paula would have built it wrongly
choices.why: She would have built exactly what was asked; the problem was in what was asked.

choices.text: The review would have rejected it
choices.why: The lesson says it would have passed review, which is why the failure would have been invisible.

choices.text: The `sent_at` column did not exist in the reminder service
choices.why: Nothing says the column was missing; the guess about the cause was what was wrong.

prompt: Which are tests the lesson gives for spotting a task disguised as an outcome? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The person would need to come back if the first idea failed
choices.why: Yes: with a task the plan was the manager’s.

choices.text: It has no deadline
choices.why: A missing deadline is a gap in the context, not the mark of a task.

choices.text: It names a mechanism such as a table or a library
choices.why: Yes: then the design has been decided for the person.

choices.text: It could be done exactly as written and still fail
choices.why: Yes: the `sent_at` check could; “exactly one reminder” could not.

choices.text: It is shorter than three sentences
choices.why: Length says nothing; an outcome can be one line.

prompt: What did Marquet ask his officers to start their proposals with?

choices.text: “I intend to…”
choices.why: Right: the officer states the plan, and over time why it is safe, and the commander checks it.

choices.text: “Permission to…”, so the commander can approve each step before it happens
choices.why: That keeps the thinking with the commander, which is what he stopped doing.

choices.text: “What should I do about…”
choices.why: A question hands the decision back up; the point was for the officer to decide.

choices.text: A written risk assessment for the operation
choices.why: He asked for intent first; the reason it was safe came with it over time.

prompt: Match each heading of Renata’s delegation with what she wrote under it for the reminders work.
hint: Five headings; one right-hand item belongs to none.

pairs.right: one reminder per appointment, and an alert if not
patients ignore the messages; two clinics complained
no change to the message text legal approved
the cause, the design, whether it needs a migration
Helena has the complaints; Yara wrote the reschedule code

right_distractors: I think it might be the `sent_at` check

prompt: Why are the limits the part of the context only the manager can supply?

choices.text: Because setting limits is how the manager keeps control of the design
choices.why: Limits are constraints from outside, not a way to steer the design; the design was Paula’s.

choices.text: Because the person would set limits that are too loose
choices.why: Nothing suggests Paula would be careless; she simply lacked the information.

choices.text: They are facts the person has no way of knowing
choices.why: Right: Paula could not have known that legal had approved the message text.

choices.text: Because company policy says only managers may write limits
choices.why: No such policy appears; the reason is who holds the facts.

prompt: A manager delegating a slow-page problem adds: “I think it’s probably the ORM doing N+1 queries.” What does the lesson advise?
hint: A guess from your manager is hard to discard.

choices.text: Put it first, since it saves the person time
choices.why: Leading with it makes it the starting point, which is the risk the lesson describes.

choices.text: Turn it into the outcome: “remove the N+1 queries”
choices.why: That is a task naming a mechanism, the opposite of an outcome.

choices.text: Leave it out, or label it a hypothesis and put it after the outcome
choices.why: Right: the person will otherwise start there and struggle to let go of it, even against the evidence.

choices.text: Keep it, as long as the deadline also carries a reason the person can weigh against what they find
choices.why: A reason for the deadline is good advice, but it does nothing about an anchoring guess.

prompt: At which of Appelo’s levels does the person decide and tell the manager afterwards?

choices.text: Inquire
choices.why: Right: at inquire the person decides, and the manager asks, or hears, afterwards.

choices.text: Advise, where the manager gives a view before the decision
choices.why: At advise the person hears the manager first, then decides.

choices.text: Consult
choices.why: At consult the manager still decides, after asking.

choices.text: Delegate, the top rung of the ladder
choices.why: At delegate the manager does not need to hear at all.

prompt: Put Appelo’s seven levels of delegation in order, from the manager deciding alone to the person deciding alone.
hint: Authority moves across in the middle.
trap: Consult and advise are easy to swap: at consult the manager decides, at advise the person does.

prompt: Paula has worked on the reminder service for a year, and a wrong fix can be reverted the same day. Which rung did Renata choose for the design, and why?
hint: Familiar and cheap to get wrong.

choices.text: Agree, because a fix that touches production should always need two people to consent
choices.why: Agree is slow and kept for decisions that really need two people; this one did not.

choices.text: Consult, since Renata was still new as a manager
choices.why: The rung depends on the decision and the person, not on how new the manager is.

choices.text: Inquire: familiar work and a cheap mistake sit high
choices.why: Right: level 6, because the two questions, cost and familiarity, both pointed up.

choices.text: Tell, so Paula would not waste time
choices.why: Telling hands over the typing, which is the task version the lesson started by rejecting.

prompt: A manager thinks a decision was delegated at advise. The engineer thinks it was at delegate, decides, and says nothing. What does the lesson say prevents this?
hint: One more line under the five headings.

choices.text: Never delegating above consult until trust is built
choices.why: That keeps the manager as a bottleneck; the problem was that the rung was never said.

choices.text: Saying the rung in words when delegating
choices.why: Right: “show me before it goes live” is advise, and saying it costs one sentence.

choices.text: A weekly status report from every engineer on the team
choices.why: A report might surface it later, but it would not have stopped the mismatch.

choices.text: Reversing the engineer’s decision quietly, to make the point
choices.why: The lesson calls a silent reversal the worst version, because it teaches that the rung meant nothing.

prompt: What does the lesson say a manager should do before correcting delegated work that looks wrong?
hint: Renata did it in the pull request.

choices.text: Offer to pair
choices.why: The lesson calls that the same rescue with better manners.

choices.text: Comment with the fix she has in mind
choices.why: That was her first instinct, and it would have replaced a correct fix with a wrong one.

choices.text: Move the work down the ladder to tell
choices.why: Changing the rung is for real trouble, said openly; here a question was enough.

choices.text: Ask what the person found and why they chose that approach
choices.why: Right: Paula’s answer revealed the reschedule cause, and the work only looked wrong because Renata’s model was.

prompt: Marcos was stuck for two weeks on a delegated upgrade and said nothing. What would have surfaced it in days?

choices.text: Delegating at a higher rung, so he felt more ownership
choices.why: He was already at the top rung; ownership was not what was missing.

choices.text: Not delegating library upgrades at all
choices.why: Routine work is a good thing to delegate; the failure was the absence of any checkpoint.

choices.text: An early checkpoint agreed when the work was delegated
choices.why: Right: the early checkpoint catches the person who is stuck before they have been stuck for long.

choices.text: Asking him every day how it was going, even though that would feel like supervision to most people
choices.why: Daily unplanned questions are the supervision the lesson distinguishes from a checkpoint.

prompt: In which situations does the lesson say taking delegated work back is right? Choose all that apply.
hint: Said openly, with the rung changed.

choices.text: A real date is about to be missed
choices.why: Yes, said openly and with the rung changed.

choices.text: The approach differs from the one the manager would take
choices.why: No: that is the rescue the lesson warns against.

choices.text: The person asks for somebody else to take over
choices.why: Yes: that is help they asked for.

choices.text: The pull request is bigger than expected
choices.why: No: size alone was what alarmed Renata, wrongly.

choices.text: A security or data-protection problem is being introduced
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Yara will lead the migration of booking data to a new schema, a month of work she has never done before, with a date the clinics were promised. Which arrangement fits the lesson best?

choices.text: Delegate at the top rung and check at the end, to show trust
choices.why: That is the disappearance, and on unfamiliar work with a date it is how Marcos’s two lost weeks happen.

choices.text: Outcome with full context, design at advise, a checkpoint early, weekly ones and one at halfway
choices.why: Right: an unfamiliar and expensive decision sits lower, and a dated, long piece of work wants the early, weekly and halfway checkpoints.

choices.text: A detailed task list written by Renata
choices.why: Tasks keep the thinking with the manager; Yara is senior and the work needs her judgement.

choices.text: Agree on every decision, so nothing goes wrong
choices.why: Agree on everything is slow and makes Renata a bottleneck; few of the decisions need two people.
